idiom_name: Data.define event object + subscriber registry / ActiveSupport::Notifications
implementation_notes: Data.define (Ruby 3.2+) creates an immutable value class in one line: members are read-only, no writers are generated, and updates return a new instance via with, which is exactly the immutability an event needs and removes the hand-written Event class plus attr_reader boilerplate. Delivery in a Rails application is ActiveSupport::Notifications: instrument("order.placed", payload) publishes and subscribe("order.placed") or a regex pattern registers consumers, passing an Event object (name, started/finished timestamps, unique_id, payload) - a ready-made event message with the timestamp the pattern asks for. Outside Rails a small subscriber registry plays the same role, and the wire form carries the event name plus a payload hash, decoded against the Data class per name.
code_sketch:
OrderPlaced = Data.define(:order_id, :occurred_at)   # immutable, no writers, #with for copies

ActiveSupport::Notifications.instrument("order.placed", order_id: order.id, occurred_at: Time.now.utc)

ActiveSupport::Notifications.subscribe(/^order\./) do |event|
  index.upsert(event.payload[:order_id])             # event.name, timestamps, payload
end

# outside Rails: registry of subscribers keyed by event class, same publish/fan-out shape
pitfalls: Data members reference mutable objects, so Data.define is shallowly immutable like every other shallow-frozen type.

A subscriber block that raises propagates into the instrumenting call site (and, in Rails, into the request that published it) - rescue inside the subscriber unless failure is meant to abort the publisher.
Event names are strings/regexes: a typo subscribes to nothing, so keep them in constants and test the wiring.
Subscribers registered at load time are never removed; long-lived processes accumulate them unless the returned subscription object is used to unsubscribe.
